loved.evidence: PM4Py has full OCEL 2.0 compatibility for object-centric event logs in both relational and XML formats — researchers appreciate it being the most up-to-date open-source library on the emerging standard (ocel-standard.org tool support page).

loved.point: ProM's breadth of algorithms / plugin ecosystem
loved.evidence: ProM's hundreds of plugins are praised as the 'gold standard for researchers' with algorithms unavailable elsewhere (fitgap.com, ProcessMind). Academics choose it specifically because commercial tools don't expose algorithm internals.

loved.point: Zero licensing cost / sovereignty
loved.evidence: Open-source tools are consistently recommended for 'flexibility and cost savings' when enterprise pricing ($5k–$150k+ licenses, $1M+ for COEs) is prohibitive. ProM is GPL; PM4Py also GPL. This is the primary switching driver from Celonis/IBM (decisions.com 2024 pricing guide).

loved.point: Apromore's visual UI for non-coders
loved.evidence: Apromore is called 'Best for Balanced Analytics and Usability' and praised for letting business users do process discovery and conformance without IT help (ProcessMind 2026 list, processmining-software.com comparison).

loved.point: bupaR's R-ecosystem fit for statisticians
loved.evidence: Researchers in academia who live in R value bupaR's tight tidyverse integration and its ability to combine process mining with statistical methods not available in PM4Py (r-bloggers.com introduction, bupaR CRAN page).

hated.point: ProM's catastrophic memory consumption on any non-trivial log
hated.evidence: Documented: a 17 MB event log triggered java.lang.OutOfMemoryError even with 5 GB heap. A 1 GB uncompressed XML log can consume >5 GB heap. The XESLite workaround exists but is 'painfully slow' (felix mannhardt blog, referenced via arxiv 2401.14149).

hated.point: ProM installation is a multi-step nightmare, especially on Mac
hated.evidence: On Mac: 'The application can't be opened' gatekeeper errors, requiring CLI workarounds. On Windows: Package Manager 'ran so slowly with repetitive messages that users questioned whether it was functioning.' Network interruptions force complete reinstallation with no resume. 'Initial navigation and first steps are far from intuitive.' (cmhstudies.com ProM review)

hated.point: ProM plugin overload — 200+ plugins with no guidance on which to use
hated.evidence: From PMC11646219 practitioner survey: 'If you go for ProM, you don't know what plugins to use.' Historical documentation confirms users were 'overwhelmed by the many plug-ins (over 200).' Five different versions of the Social Network miner exist. Plugin quality 'has noticeably declined' in ProM 6 (fluxicon.com ProM 6 critique).

hated.point: ProM is designed for academic researchers, not practitioners
hated.evidence: Fluxicon (Disco makers) wrote 'Why We Hate ProM 6' in 2010 — still cited: missing conformance checker, missing performance analysis plugin, no Mac installer, interface is 'gray which intuitively implies unimplemented,' focus on research advancement over practitioner problems. These issues persist in 2024.

hated.point: PM4Py has no built-in GUI / web interface — pure library
hated.evidence: PM4Py is a library only. Business analysts cannot use it without Python skills. Commercial comparison articles consistently note 'not as user-friendly as commercial platforms' and it is only usable 'in both academia and industry projects' by those with 'technical expertise' (ProcessMind, pm4py paper 1905.06169).

hated.point: PM4Py single-threaded performance: most algorithms run on one core
hated.evidence: Academic paper (PM4Py-GPU, arxiv 2204.04898) explicitly states 'most of its algorithms work in single-thread, which is a drawback for performance.' Only a new inductive miner variant adds multiprocessing; other algorithms remain serial. GPU version requires NVIDIA RAPIDS, a niche setup.

hated.point: PM4Py graphviz dependency hell breaks visualization in most environments
hated.evidence: Top GitHub issues include 'Failed to install python-graphviz' (#2, pm4py-core), 'Graphviz executables not found' (#96, both repos), 'pm4py no visualization' on Databricks. System PATH configuration, conda conflicts, and Windows incompatibilities are recurring. Databricks and cloud notebook environments are especially broken.

hated.point: ETL / data connectors are essentially non-existent in open source
hated.evidence: PMC survey quote: 'ETL functionality in process mining tools is lacking. Very often this happens outside of the process mining tools and you are on your own there.' No SAP connector, no database connectors, no built-in ERP integration for any open-source tool. Only a niche sap-extractor Python package exists (arxiv 2110.03467).

hated.point: XES format is an obstacle: CSV import is painful and error-prone
hated.evidence: XES is the native format but CSV is what everyone has. Research paper (CEUR Vol-3758/paper-24.pdf) documents that automated CSV ingestion remains a hard problem: encoding detection, separator detection, case/activity/timestamp column identification, and timestamp format parsing all fail without guidance. Tools provide minimal help.

hated.point: Apromore Community/Core Edition strips out critical features vs. Enterprise
hated.evidence: processmining-software.com comparison: CE has 'Only 1 custom dashboard possible,' 'Filtering only by activities, not by transitions,' 'No further dedicated collaboration features.' Conformance checking in CE is 'additional plugin, provided on demand' per Apromore forum (forum.apromore.org thread #62). Basic auth only (no SSO/LDAP enterprise options).

hated.point: No commercial support — users are on their own
hated.evidence: Enterprise pricing guide (decisions.com) explicitly contrasts ProM's GPL license as 'without vendor support or advanced features.' Academic maintainers respond slowly; production incidents have no SLA. This is a blocker for regulated industries and production deployments.

hated.point: PM4Py API breaking changes and deprecation churn
hated.evidence: Changelog shows repeated deprecations: read_petri_net removed, format_dataframe behavior changed, get_attributes renamed to get_event_attributes. OCPA pin trap (pm4py drifting to 2.2.32 can't read OCEL 2.0) — documented in project memory. Downstream projects break silently on library upgrades.

missing_or_frustrating.point: No out-of-the-box web UI / dashboard for business users on top of pm4py
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Repeatedly identified gap: PM4Py is 'just a library.' Multiple comparison articles say the market is shifting toward 'self-service, SMB-friendly' platforms but no mature open-source web app wraps PM4Py for non-coders. Jupyter notebooks are the closest, which excludes 80% of process mining end-users.

missing_or_frustrating.point: No automated data ingestion / ETL pipeline — data prep is 60–80% of project time
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Practitioner survey (PMC11646219): 'data pre-processing is recognized as one of the most time-consuming aspects of process mining projects, with many projects spending 60-80% of their efforts on this task, while some up to 90%.' Open-source tools provide no guided data preparation workflow.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Root cause analysis / AI-guided analysis is absent from open source
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: PMC11646219: 'Missing implementations of root cause analysis, hierarchical discovery, and automated data ingestion limit analytical capabilities.' Commercial tools (Celonis) offer AI-recommended next actions; open-source tools show you the DFG and leave you to interpret it yourself.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Predictive process monitoring / cases-at-risk is enterprise-only
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: 40% of process mining license deals include predictive tools (Gartner 2024), but PM4Py's predictive module is limited to research prototypes. No open-source tool offers a production-ready predictive monitoring dashboard with SHAP explanations.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Real-time / streaming process mining has no usable open-source interface
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: PM4Py has a streaming module documented but it is a library-only component with no UI. Commercial tools offer live dashboards and alerting. This gap leaves practitioners doing batch-only analysis even when their use case requires continuous monitoring.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Process simulation is missing or rudimentary in all open-source tools
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Only Apromore Enterprise offers simulation. Apromore's own marketing notes it 'lags behind some competitors in actionable automation features.' PM4Py has no simulation. ProM has simulation plugins but they are poorly maintained and hard to use.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Guidance on which analysis to run and how to interpret results
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: PMC11646219: 'Lack of training materials for advanced topics in process mining' and 'no help or indication on pre-processing of the event log is given to users, and there is no support for any explanation.' Open-source tools dump algorithms on users with no interpretive scaffolding.

missing_or_frustrating.point: DFG spaghetti with no automated simplification or variant management
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: PMC practitioner survey: 'DFG shortcomings prevent proper representation of concurrent behavior and can display non-existent paths.' No open-source tool has meaningful automated DFG simplification, variant filtering, or happy-path extraction built into its UI.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Multi-table / multi-system event log construction (OCEL) is research-only
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Extracting cross-system event logs requires custom SQL joins. OCEL 2.0 support exists in PM4Py but there is no guided wizard. ProM has no OCEL 2.0 support in stable builds (ocel-standard.org). bupaR has no OCEL support at all.

missing_or_frustrating.point: SSO/LDAP/enterprise auth and RBAC missing from community editions
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Apromore CE offers only 'Basic; LDAP' auth. No SSO, no role-based access control, no audit logs. For compliance-sensitive industries this is a hard blocker for self-hosting (processmining-software.com comparison).

The total cost of a process mining project (including 12–24 months implementation, multiple FTEs) is often 3–5x the license cost — open source just relocates this cost to internal engineering time
switch_drivers: Switch TO open source: Celonis/IBM pricing is out of reach for SMBs and mid-market; open-source provides the same algorithms at zero license cost
Switch TO open source: need for full algorithmic customization that commercial GUI tools do not expose (PM4Py cited explicitly for this use case)
Switch TO open source: data sovereignty and compliance requirements — no data leaves the premises
Switch TO open source: academic/research use cases where ProM's algorithm breadth is unmatched commercially
Switch AWAY from ProM: memory crashes on production-scale logs, no Mac installer, plugin chaos — practitioners move to Disco (commercial) or PM4Py
Switch AWAY from pm4py: no UI — business analysts cannot use it; teams that outgrow notebooks move to Apromore or commercial tools
Switch AWAY from Apromore CE: feature wall — conformance checking, multi-dashboard, connectors locked in enterprise tier; teams either pay or move to pm4py for full control
Stay on open source: after initial Celonis pilot, procurement complexity, consultant dependency, and price escalation lead teams back to self-hosted open source
Switch TO FlowMiner-style tools: fills the gap between 'just a Python library' (pm4py) and 'full enterprise suite' (Celonis) — web UI, managed deployment, no coding required

research.scope: General process-mining buyer and practitioner pain points, independent of vendor: why projects fail or stall, time-to-value problems, data extraction and ETL pain (especially SAP), event-log preparation difficulty, low user adoption, insight-to-action gaps, and change management failures. Sources include academic practitioner studies (PMC/Springer), Fluxicon practitioner camp notes, Deloitte/HFS/PwC surveys, ProcessMaker/Mavim/BPM-d blogs, Celonis/PeerSpot reviews, and altexsoft/CKM Analytix deep-dives.

loved.point: Process transparency and discovery when data is clean
loved.evidence: When event data is well-structured, practitioners report it surfaces problems invisible to traditional BI dashboards — variants, rework loops, and wait-time bottlenecks (AltexSoft blog, Fluxicon camp notes 2024)

loved.point: Objective, data-driven evidence for process arguments
loved.evidence: Analysts value that process mining eliminates internal political battles about 'how things really work' by showing actual execution paths rather than assumed ones (BPM-d blog; multiple Deloitte survey respondents; 80% in Deloitte 2025 survey agreed it delivers added value)

loved.point: Conformance checking for compliance validation
loved.evidence: Finance and audit teams specifically appreciate the ability to check actual execution against prescribed process models (AIMulitple trends overview; Deloitte 2025 survey)

loved.point: pm4py as a free, Python-native research/prototyping tool
loved.evidence: PM4Py downloaded over 1 million times; widely used in academia and for custom pipelines where commercial licensing is a blocker (Semantic Scholar / pm4py.fit.fraunhofer.de publications list)

loved.point: Scalable insight across millions of process instances simultaneously
loved.evidence: Practitioners note the fundamental advantage over manual process audit: ability to analyze entire populations of cases rather than handpicked samples (ProcessMind blog; AltexSoft blog)

hated.point: Data/ETL preparation consumes 60–80% of total project time
hated.evidence: 'Event log extraction takes up 80% of the time in the entire process mining project' — validated by multiple surveys; SAP blog (2022) confirms 81% of respondents say event log extraction is the dominant time sink. Academic review (MDPI 2021) puts data pre-processing at 60–90% of effort.

hated.point: SAP event log extraction is uniquely painful — many tables, no turnkey open-source support
hated.evidence: Extracting from SAP ERP 'involves many different tables/objects'; open-source ETL support is scarce; commercial vendors maintain connectors for only a limited number of processes in an ad-hoc manner. Convergence/divergence problems from case notion choices plague SAP logs (arxiv 2110.03467; AltexSoft blog).

hated.point: Insight-to-action gap: findings sit on dashboards, nothing changes
hated.evidence: 'The story stays on the dashboard. The insight is generated, acknowledged, and then left sitting at the level of observation while day-to-day operations continue much as before.' (BPM-d blog) — Process mining camp 2024 identified this as challenge OC3; Mavim 2025 blog calls it 'buried in dashboards, but nothing changes'. HFS Research found over 2-in-3 process intelligence initiatives 'led to disappointing results or under-delivered on promise'.

hated.point: Lack of clear ownership: process insights span multiple functions, nobody acts
hated.evidence: 'Insights that span multiple functions fall into a gap between teams, with each function acknowledging the problem but none taking responsibility for resolving it.' (BPM-d blog) — cited as a primary stall reason alongside risk aversion. Mavim pitfall #6: findings remain 'interesting but unused' without ownership.

hated.point: Data quality problems cascade into wrong conclusions
hated.evidence: 78% of practitioners report data quality issues as a challenge (PMC 11646219 survey of 41 analysts); esystems.fi blog: 'many teams run into delays or wrong conclusions because they skip the step of cleaning their event logs'; missing timestamps, inconsistent activity naming, duplicate records, and clock mismatches all documented.

hated.point: Spaghetti models: process maps too complex for non-experts to read
hated.evidence: 'Mining event logs usually results in models which contain an overwhelming amount of behavior (spaghetti models) that make it hard to identify specific paths.' (multiple academic sources). Fluxicon camp 2024 PC1 challenge: processes appear 'quite chaotic when you first look at their complete picture'. Gartner review of Celonis notes 'too many bugs and no consistent front-end development of features'.

hated.point: Domain knowledge bottleneck: analysts hit a wall without subject matter experts
hated.evidence: C20 (Process Domain Understanding) was the single most-cited challenge in the 41-analyst PMC study (82% experienced it). Fluxicon camp 2024 PC4: practitioners 'hit a wall needing subject matter experts to interpret patterns'. C14 (Access to Additional Information) ranked #1 by mean relevancy score (80.48/100).

hated.point: Source system knowledge gap: no data catalog, undocumented table structures
hated.evidence: C7 (Source System Knowledge) affected 83% of analysts in PMC study: 'Most systems require knowledge, and I am not an expert'. Lack of data catalogs and documentation for tables is a primary blocker (Fluxicon camp DC1).

hated.point: Scope and question formulation uncertainty: practitioners don't know where to start
hated.evidence: C1 (Question Formulation) affected 89% of analysts and had the lowest solvability rate (54%) in the PMC study. Mavim pitfall #5: overly complex scope leads to teams being 'buried in exceptions'. ProcessMind: 'without a clear understanding of which processes to focus on, effort becomes scattered'.

hated.point: Analysis paralysis: overwhelming volume of insights without actionable focus
hated.evidence: Mavim 2025: 'analysis paralysis can lead to frustration and ultimately, abandonment of the project'. BPM-d blog: organizations 'buried in dashboards, but nothing changes'. C17 (Analysis Focus) in PMC study: losing sight of original question amid details.

hated.point: Data access and regulatory/security barriers block projects before they start
hated.evidence: C6 (Data Access) affected 89% of analysts and ranked #2 by relevancy score (79.56/100) in PMC study. Fluxicon camp DC4: 'organizational reluctance to share data due to security fears and misuse concerns'; GDPR compliance adds complexity. Privacy literature notes 'companies are reluctant to share private information required to execute process mining algorithms'.

hated.point: Process mining treated as IT project rather than business transformation
hated.evidence: Mavim pitfall #3: 'value doesn't emerge without connecting insights to business outcomes'. ProcessMaker/Decisions blog lists this as primary failure reason. Deloitte 2025: 'lack of management attention' jumped to 41% (from 26% in 2021) — front-line sees value but leadership doesn't.

hated.point: Timestamp headaches: different systems, time zones, local vs. UTC recording
hated.evidence: CKM Analytix deep-dive documents format inconsistencies (e.g., NYC vs. Phoenix timestamps), daylight savings complications, semantic ambiguity about whether timestamp marks start/middle/end of step, and unknown pre-processing already applied to data.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Turnkey, open-source SAP/ERP event log extractors
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: 'Open-source support for ETL is scarce, while commercial vendors maintain connectors to ERP systems for only a limited number of processes in an ad-hoc manner' (arxiv 2110.03467). SAP Community Q&A threads show practitioners still manually scripting extractions. This is a major market gap flagged by practitioners.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Guided, opinionated methodology for scope selection and project setup
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: C1 (Question Formulation) is the hardest unsolved challenge (54% solvability). Fluxicon camp PC3: practitioners want 'structured 12-step project guidance'. Without methodology, POCs get stuck at 'find something interesting' rather than a defined business question.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Actionable recommendations, not just diagnostic dashboards
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: BPM-d blog: 'academic research supports that practitioners face seven distinct challenges progressing from insights to improvements, with methodologies focusing almost entirely on obtaining insights rather than translating them into action.' Skan.ai: tools that only analyze historical data and cannot prevent issues in real-time are seen as underperforming.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Self-service tools accessible to business users without data engineering support
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: ProcessMind launched SMB-targeted self-service tool explicitly to address this gap (PEX Network); AltexSoft: 52% of companies cite 'lack of expertise or tooling' as primary deployment blocker (PwC study). Market is visibly shifting toward self-service but most tools still require data engineers.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Cross-system case ID linking without manual bridging
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Nick Blackbourn Medium article: 'different IT systems may use different identifiers for the same order as it moves through website, warehouse, and shipment company — organizations must locate bridging information.' No automated solution exists for most organizations.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Real-time / continuous monitoring rather than periodic batch analysis
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Skan.ai sign #5: 'only analyzes historical data; cannot prevent issues in real-time — conformance violations surface in review cycles, not beforehand.' Practitioners want forward-looking monitoring, not just post-mortem analysis.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Object-centric process mining (OCEL) tooling that doesn't require PhD-level setup
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: IBM arxiv paper (2512.03906) discusses that OCEL approaches remain research-stage for most practitioners; flattening SAP object-centric data to traditional event logs causes convergence/divergence artifacts but OCEL tooling is immature.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Feedback loops: did the process change after recommendations?
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Fluxicon camp OC3: 'preventing processes from reverting to old patterns after improvements' is an identified gap. BPM-d: 'required: feedback loops monitoring whether changes achieved intended effects' — no mainstream tool handles this well.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Affordable entry point for SMBs and teams without $150K+ annual budgets
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: ProcessMind explicitly launched a new SMB platform because the gap exists. PeerSpot Celonis reviews: starting at $15K/year but scaling to $200K+. Implementation adds $50K–$100K per process in year 1. SMBs and mid-market companies cannot justify this.

ux_complaints: Spaghetti models are the default output for complex processes; new users are immediately overwhelmed and cannot derive actionable conclusions without weeks of filtering experience (Fluxicon camp PC1; multiple academic sources)

Complex filter UX: even experienced users struggle with 'losing sight of original question amid details' (PMC study C17, 50% affected); tools don't scaffold the analyst's journey from question to insight

Sharing insights outside the platform requires cumbersome export processes — dashboards are not stakeholder-ready for CFO/COO level (Skan.ai sign #4: 'generic views rather than stakeholder-specific configurations')

Steep learning curve for tool functionality (PMC study C11: 55% experience unfamiliarity with specific tool functions); C23 (Enablement and Training) affected 67% with 'limited access to quality training'
Conformance checking results are 'difficult to interpret for users in a business context' (arxiv 2007.10903) — presented as technical alignment scores rather than actionable business language
Time to first insight exceeds six months in many implementations due to complex system integrations and event log extraction requirements (Skan.ai sign #3 quoting practitioners)
Process mining tools surface insights but deliver them in formats difficult to share with decision-makers, creating a translation problem (Skan.ai sign #4)

Celonis-specific: 'filter bar in views cannot be resized; maximum 15 filters create workflow bottlenecks'; 'Copilot feature occasionally freezes, requiring restart'; 'complex programming needs and frequent updates strain user adoption' (PeerSpot reviews)

Per-user AND per-GB data pricing: 'Every user has an additional charge, and every gig of data you bring in costs extra' (PeerSpot Solutions Architect reviewer2079900)

52% of non-adopters cite 'unavailability of process mining tooling or expertise' as the primary blocker — which translates to consulting dependency for implementation (PwC study via multiple secondary sources)
Building a process mining Center of Excellence requires 15+ dedicated full-time employees at minimum; largest teams exceed 150 people (ProcessMaker/Decisions blog)
Implementations commonly require 12–24 months before value delivery — creating a long payback period that many organizations abandon mid-way (ProcessMaker/Decisions blog)
IBM Process Mining starts at $3,200/month for one analyst and 20 million events — consumption-based pricing creates unpredictable costs at scale (ProcessMaker/Decisions 2024 pricing guide)

Consultants report difficulty convincing stakeholders to fund process mining because 'stakeholders could not clearly distinguish between process mining and business intelligence' — value proposition confusion (PMC study)
Data integration labor and Center of Excellence establishment costs can equal or exceed the first-year software license cost (CheckThat.ai Celonis pricing analysis)
switch_drivers: Organizations choose commercial tools (Celonis, UiPath, SAP Signavio) for pre-built ERP connectors that reduce the 80% data-prep time overhead — the connector library is the primary differentiator
Organizations stay with their process mining vendor due to sunk-cost investment in data pipelines, training, and CoE headcount — switching costs are very high once pipelines are built

Organizations leave Celonis for cheaper alternatives (ARIS, SAP Signavio) primarily due to cost: 'the most expensive solution in the market' with many customers 'ready to migrate to more affordable solutions' (PeerSpot Celonis reviews)

Privacy/data sovereignty concerns push some organizations toward on-premises or open-source solutions: 'companies are reluctant to share private information required to execute process mining algorithms with external parties' (academic literature; Fluxicon camp DC4)

Organizations that fail to achieve insight-to-action results eventually shelve the tool: HFS Research found over 2-in-3 process intelligence initiatives under-delivered; Mavim notes teams 'abandon the project' after analysis paralysis
Teams that start with pm4py for prototyping hit the limits of manual ETL and visualization, driving them toward commercial tools or custom platform builds
SMBs are locked out of top-tier tools entirely by pricing, creating demand for self-service affordable alternatives (ProcessMind SMB launch; gap explicitly called out by market)
Lack of internal expertise is a forcing function toward consultant-driven implementations — which then creates dependency and cost escalation that can itself become a reason to abandon the initiative

research.scope: Cross-vendor process mining pricing, licensing, procurement, and lock-in sentiment — focused on Celonis, SAP Signavio, Apromore, IBM, UiPath, and the open-source/self-hosted alternative opportunity (June 2026)

loved.point: Celonis delivers measurable ROI for large ERP-heavy enterprises
loved.evidence: Multiple Gartner and PeerSpot reviewers acknowledge Celonis works at enterprise scale; vendor-cited 383% three-year ROI (Forrester TEI) and case studies showing 80% efficiency gains cited positively by satisfied accounts. Several named accounts (Accenture $35M P2P, Deutsche Telekom €40M/yr) are held up as proof points. PeerSpot.

loved.point: SAP Signavio respected for collaboration and ease-of-use pre-acquisition
loved.evidence: Reviewers on PeerSpot called Signavio 'much greater value than what we paid for' and praised process modeling collaboration. Satisfaction was higher before SAP's price increases. PeerSpot/Capterra.

loved.point: IBM Process Mining praised for transparent, lower entry-point pricing
loved.evidence: TrustRadius reviewer stated 'Celonis license cost is ten times higher' than IBM. IBM publishes prices ($3,200/month for 1 analyst + 20M events; $33K-$51K/year published tiers) which buyers appreciate as a baseline for ROI math. TrustRadius/IBM pricing page.

loved.point: ProcessMind and Mindzie praised for SMB-accessible transparent pricing
loved.evidence: ProcessMind at $99-$199/month with no hidden fees cited by multiple comparison sites as the primary appeal for budget-constrained SMBs displaced by Celonis pricing. ProcessMind comparison blog.

loved.point: Apromore praised as a capable open-source alternative to Celonis for mid-market
loved.evidence: Gartner Peer Insights and G2 users call Apromore 'a full-featured, advanced process mining platform comparable with much more expensive proprietary options.' Recognized as Everest Group PEAK Matrix Leader two years running. Apromore/G2.

hated.point: Celonis pricing is opaque and negotiation is adversarial
hated.evidence: Gartner Peer Insights rates Celonis 4.1/5 on 'Evaluation and Contracting' — its lowest dimension — specifically reflecting pricing opacity and negotiation complexity. The pricing page redirects to a contact form with no tier names or price ranges. CheckThat.ai/Gartner.

hated.point: Celonis total cost of ownership is prohibitive for all but very large enterprises
hated.evidence: Year 1 TCO documented at $470K-$1.5M+: base license $150K-$250K, implementation $120K-$500K, CoE staffing $200K-$700K. Forrester composite customer paid $1.57M Year 1 scaling to $11.42M three-year TCO. Ernst & Young senior manager called it 'the most expensive solution in the market.' PeerSpot/CheckThat.ai/Forrester.

hated.point: Per-process licensing actively blocks experimentation and expansion
hated.evidence: Gartner Peer Insights reviewer: 'The current licensing model sometimes limits ambitious value goals, as we can't experiment with building analyses in different areas without a long-term license for that process.' Each Order-to-Cash, P2P, AP process requires separate licensing. Costs scaled from $1.26M (4 processes) to $5.25M (12 processes) by Year 3 in Forrester case. CheckThat.ai/Gartner.

hated.point: Non-cancelable, non-refundable contracts with no downgrade rights create lock-in
hated.evidence: 'Celonis subscriptions are non-cancelable and non-refundable during the committed term' and 'no downgrades are permitted, only upgrades.' Auto-renewal clauses are present and must be actively negotiated out. Vendr/CheckThat.ai.

hated.point: Center of Excellence consulting dependency makes ROI unreachable without heavy services spend
hated.evidence: Celonis's own research shows customers with a CoE are 8.8x more likely to achieve positive returns, yet a 3-5 FTE CoE costs $400K-$700K annually. Implementation fees frequently equal or exceed the first-year license. The practical message: you cannot succeed without paying consulting fees that can dwarf the software cost. CheckThat.ai.

hated.point: SAP Signavio prices spiked sharply after SAP acquisition, pricing out SMBs
hated.evidence: 'After SAP acquired Signavio, the prices increased significantly, making it too expensive for our small company to afford.' — Sandrine Pluvinot, Altitude Infrastructure (PeerSpot). Another reviewer called enterprise license costs 'extortionate' at ~£150K-£200K/year. PeerSpot.

hated.point: SAP Signavio requires separate licenses for process modeling vs process mining modules
hated.evidence: Fidelity International reviewer: 'Mining had to be purchased separately — if we were already paying for Process Manager, we should have access to analyze it as well.' PeerSpot.

hated.point: Data volume-based pricing (APC) creates unpredictable cost escalation
hated.evidence: Celonis charges on Analytics Processing Capacity (data volume in bytes) with undisclosed tier boundaries. A Solutions Architect reviewer: 'Every user has additional charge; every gig of data costs extra.' Plan for 20-30% headroom above projected volumes to avoid mid-contract penalties. PeerSpot/CheckThat.ai.

hated.point: Celonis platform is cloud-only — no full on-premise option for regulated industries
hated.evidence: Celonis docs confirm the platform itself operates as a cloud service; on-premise extractors act as a bridge but raw data must transit to Celonis Cloud. Organizations in banking, insurance, and government requiring full data residency or air-gapped deployments are structurally excluded. Celonis docs/CheckThat.ai.

hated.point: Realistic payback timeline is 9-21 months, far longer than vendor's <6 month claim
hated.evidence: G2 data from 322 reviews shows 21-month average payback versus Forrester's vendor-funded <6-month projection. Gap attributed to smaller deployments and immature CoE structures. Buyers who signed on the strength of fast payback claims feel misled. CheckThat.ai/G2.

missing_or_frustrating.point: A pricing model that does not charge per process — buyers want unlimited-process access
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: The per-process licensing model is the single most-cited structural complaint. Gartner reviewer explicitly said it 'limits ambitious value goals.' ProcessMind and Mindzie win SMB customers specifically by advertising no process count limits. Gartner Peer Insights/ProcessMind blog.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Published, transparent pricing so buyers can build a business case without a sales call
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Celonis and SAP Signavio both require contacting sales; IBM and ProcessMind publish prices and win deals partly on that transparency alone. Buyers consistently ask for a rate card. Vendr/CheckThat.ai/multiple comparison sources.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Ability to self-host or run fully on-premise for data sovereignty and compliance
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Healthcare, banking, government, and EU-regulated industries need on-premise or air-gapped deployment. Celonis cloud-only architecture structurally blocks this segment. PM4Py/ProM capture this niche today but lack a polished UI. Celonis docs/market research.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Self-service onboarding without mandatory consulting dependency
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: ProcessMind and Mindzie explicitly market 'no-code, no consultant needed' as a primary differentiator. The industry standard (Celonis, Signavio) of requiring 12-24 month implementations with partner firms is cited as a key frustration for lean teams. ProcessMind/Mindzie comparison pages.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Flat-rate or user-seat pricing that does not scale with data volume
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Volume-based pricing (Celonis APC per GB, IBM per-event tier) creates budget unpredictability. Buyers want predictable annual fees. SaaS model with per-seat flat rates is described as what makes newer entrants like ProcessMind attractive. ProcessMind pricing page/multiple sources.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Mid-market tier: $20K-$80K/year range with real capabilities — the pricing gap is empty
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: There is a documented pricing desert between free/open-source tools (ProM, pm4py) and Celonis enterprise ($150K+). IBM starts at ~$33K-$51K/year with published pricing, but this range is poorly served by vendors with serious UI and connectors. Multiple pricing guide sources.

missing_or_frustrating.point: Apromore open-source community edition sustainability post-Salesforce acquisition
missing_or_frustrating.evidence: Analyst commentary on the Salesforce-Apromore deal included: 'Hopefully this will not come as an add-on with an inflated price tag.' Community users (150+ orgs on open-source edition) are watching for price changes. Constellation Research/SalesforceBen.

ux_complaints: Celonis requires integration to every source system separately to extract data — described by Gartner reviewers as difficult to implement, requiring significant technical effort across 12-24 months.
Celonis EMS (Execution Management System) learning curve is steep for non-technical users — 'user experience complicated and challenging' per Gartner commentary.
SAP Signavio's process mining module is separate from process modeling, requiring a separate purchase and login — frustrates users who want an integrated experience.
Celonis CoE requirement effectively means organizations without a dedicated 3-5 FTE analytics team cannot succeed — gatekeeps the value behind organizational maturity not everyone has.
IBM Process Mining onboarding requires technical expertise despite published pricing — still not truly self-service.

All major vendors (Celonis, Signavio, Apromore enterprise) have lengthy procurement cycles requiring multiple sales calls, demos, and security reviews before any access is granted — no instant trial with real data.
pricing_procurement: Celonis entry price: $150K-$200K/year for a departmental pilot; enterprise $1.26M-$5.25M+/year; Year 1 TCO with implementation and CoE: $470K-$1.5M+. Source: Forrester TEI, CheckThat.ai.
Celonis real buyer data (SpendHound, 160 contracts): SMB median $2,061/year (likely Snap/free tier), enterprise median $286,356/year. One documented contract range: $6K-$130K/year.
Celonis subscriptions are non-cancelable, non-refundable, with no downgrade rights — only upgrades allowed mid-term. Auto-renewal clauses present and must be explicitly removed in negotiation.

Celonis per-process licensing: scaling from 4 to 12 processes increased annual software cost from $1.26M to $5.25M (Forrester). Blocking experimentation across process areas is the #1 licensing complaint.

SAP Signavio post-acquisition price increase: 'prices increased significantly, making it too expensive for our small company to afford.' One enterprise license cited at £150K-£200K/year with 'extortionate' characterization.
SAP Signavio: licensing structure 'unclear and complex,' data-usage-based pricing creates cost estimation uncertainty. Process Manager and Process Intelligence are separate license purchases.
IBM Process Mining: published pricing at $3,200/month (1 analyst, 20M events) to $51,000/year SaaS — approximately 3-10x cheaper than Celonis at entry. Has consumption-based and on-premise options.

Celonis consulting/implementation cost often equals or exceeds Year 1 license: Forrester documented ~$305K implementation on $1.26M software spend. Partners (Accenture, Deloitte, EY) bundle software and services separately.

Center of Excellence staffing: Celonis's own research shows 8.8x ROI uplift from a mature CoE, but building one costs $400K-$700K/year in FTE and partner fees — a hidden cost most buyers don't budget for.

Celonis 'Evaluation & Contracting' rated 4.1/5 on Gartner Peer Insights — the lowest of all capability dimensions — reflecting buyer frustration specifically with pricing opacity and negotiation complexity.

Celonis v. SAP antitrust lawsuit (filed March 2025): SAP allegedly threatened customers with high data extraction fees to coerce them into using Signavio, and offered Signavio at low/zero cost to block Celonis — illustrates how ERP data access becomes a second lock-in layer on top of license costs.

SaaS price inflation context: enterprise SaaS prices rose 12.2% in 2024 vs 2.7% inflation (4.5x gap) — Celonis renewal uplifts track this trend, with uplift resistance requiring active negotiation at contract renewal.
switch_drivers: Primary reason to choose Celonis: already heavily invested in SAP ERP and need deep connector; have budget for CoE; processing 1M+ transactions per process per year where ROI math works.

Primary reason to leave/avoid Celonis: total Year 1 cost $470K-$1.5M+ is unjustifiable for organizations under Fortune 500 scale; per-process licensing blocks experimentation; cloud-only architecture excluded by regulated-industry compliance requirements.

Primary reason to choose SAP Signavio over Celonis: already in SAP ecosystem, offered at low/zero cost as part of SAP deal (documented in Celonis antitrust complaint); ease of use for process modeling collaboration.

Primary reason to leave SAP Signavio: post-acquisition price spike described as 'too expensive for our small company'; separate license required for mining module; perceived as inferior to Celonis for deep mining.
Why IBM Process Mining wins: published pricing 3-10x cheaper than Celonis at entry; IBM relationship/existing contract; on-premise deployment option for regulated industries.
Why open-source (pm4py, ProM) wins: zero license cost; full data sovereignty; no consulting dependency for technical teams; but lacks polished UI and enterprise connectors.
Why newer SMB tools (ProcessMind $99-$199/month, Mindzie) win: transparent pricing, no consultant required, instant onboarding — the exact opposite of the Celonis procurement experience.

Apromore acquisition by Salesforce (Nov 2025): existing Salesforce customers now have a process mining option bundled in their existing spend; but community-edition users watching for open-source access to be curtailed or priced up.

Data sovereignty as a growing switch driver: Celonis cloud-only architecture is a structural barrier for EU banking/government/healthcare buyers requiring on-premise or air-gapped deployment; self-hostable open-source tools directly address this.

Pricing model preference signal: ProcessMind and Mindzie's 'unlimited processes, flat monthly fee' positioning wins explicitly because it resolves the per-process licensing complaint — the winning pricing model for buyers displaced from Celonis.
